case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the President may remove a sitting member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors notwithstanding statutory for-cause removal protections, and whether a preliminary injunction blocking that removal should be stayed pending appeal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Banking Act of 1935 § 203(b) (codified in relevant part at 12 U.S.C. § 241) providing that Federal Reserve Board of Governors members may be removed by the President only "for cause"; U.S. Constitution Article II (the Executive Power, Take Care Clause, and separation-of-powers principles implicated by presidential removal authority).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The President argues he lawfully removed Governor Lisa D. Cook based on alleged material misrepresentations connected to her mortgage (conduct characterized as at least grossly negligent and potentially fraudulent), asserting that this constitutes adequate "cause" and creates an intolerable appearance of impropriety for an official involved in monetary policy. In the stay posture, the applicants emphasize that the case can be resolved as a statutory 'for-cause' application (i.e., whether Cook’s conduct meets the removal standard) rather than a broad constitutional ruling on whether for-cause protections for Federal Reserve Governors are valid, and they ask the Supreme Court to stay the district court’s preliminary injunction preventing the removal.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Cook and supporting amici contend the district court correctly enjoined the removal and that a stay would effectively give the President the practical benefit of a merits victory by allowing immediate replacement and policy influence before appellate review concludes. They stress Congress’s deliberate design of Federal Reserve independence through meaningful for-cause limits, grounded historically and doctrinally in Supreme Court precedent approving removal protections for certain independent agencies; they argue that undermining those protections via an interim stay would nullify judicial review and subvert congressional intent even if the removal is later held unlawful.
key_precedents: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor offer the strongest point: a stay may, as a practical matter, hand the President much of the benefit of removal before appellate review, risking dilution of Congress’s for-cause design for a multimember expert body. But the injunction here is not merely status-quo preserving; as Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize, it affirmatively disables the President from exercising even arguable removal authority over an officer performing substantial executive functions, inflicting an immediate Article II injury that does not depend on proving counterfactual downstream policy changes. On likelihood of success, I agree with Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh that we should not engraft implied notice-and-hearing prerequisites or an artificially cramped, “on-the-job only” definition of cause onto § 241’s unadorned text; integrity-related material misrepresentations plausibly qualify as “cause” at this stage. If the tenure protection ultimately proves invalid, severability should follow because the Board can function independently and nothing suggests Congress preferred no Board to one with at-will removability.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s chief point—that Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener support a single for-cause layer for a multimember expert body, and that a stay would effectively hand the President the practical benefit of removal—does not answer the distinct injury here: a judicial injunction that affirmatively prevents the President from exercising supervision via removal. Even assuming § 241 is valid and enforceable as written, that order directly interferes with Article II’s vesting of the executive power and constitutes irreparable separation-of-powers harm independent of downstream policy shifts, as the Chief emphasizes. And if § 241’s for-cause restriction exceeds Congress’s power as applied to principal officers exercising substantial executive authority, the Constitution has always displaced the conflicting statutory limit; the immediate harm is the court’s restraint on the President, not any automatic taint of Board actions. Given that narrower focus, I would grant a stay pending appeal while the statutory “cause” question (and any constitutional question) is resolved.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is equitable: a stay may confer much of the practical benefit of removal before appellate review can test whether “cause” existed, potentially undermining Congress’s design. But that concern does not answer the distinct and ongoing Article II injury that Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas identify: a judicial order affirmatively compelling the President to retain a principal officer and disabling even arguably lawful supervision through removal—harm not readily cured by later merits review. On likelihood of success, I agree with Justices Gorsuch and Kavanaugh that we should not infer extra notice-and-hearing or an artificially cramped, “in-office only” notion of “cause” from statutory silence; serious integrity-related misrepresentations plausibly satisfy cause at least enough to justify interim relief. In this posture, preserving the President’s ability to execute arguable statutory removal authority (pending appeal) outweighs the risk that the stay will be difficult to unwind if the government ultimately loses on the merits.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are right to flag that an injunction can impose an Article II injury by preventing the President from acting on asserted removal authority, but that assumes the authority is plausibly within the statutory constraint Congress affirmatively enacted in § 241. Under Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener, we have long respected Congress’s choice to provide for-cause tenure protections for multimember expert bodies, and this Board’s authority is not the Seila Law paradigm of a single head wielding unilateral coercive power against private parties—diminishing the separation-of-powers urgency at the stay stage. Justice Gorsuch’s proposal to grant a stay on “narrow statutory grounds” still requires a strong likelihood that the alleged misrepresentations clearly satisfy the historically cabined understanding of “cause” Congress used to protect independence; on this preliminary record, that showing is not sufficiently clear to justify granting the practical benefit of removal before appellate review. Because the stay would be hard to unwind and could effectively nullify Congress’s for-cause design before we determine whether “cause” existed, the equities favor maintaining the injunction pending appeal.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s point that an injunction preventing removal can itself work an Article II injury, in the sense that it constrains a supervisory tool in real time. But that claim assumes the President has at least a strong likelihood of lawful removal authority under § 241 as historically understood; on this preliminary record, I do not think the government has shown that the asserted misrepresentations clearly fit within the bounded Humphrey’s Executor/Wiener conception of “cause,” rather than amounting to a discretionary policy-ground for displacement. As Justice Barrett emphasizes, a stay here would effectively grant the practical benefit of removal and replacement before appellate review can determine whether “cause” existed, a shift in the congressionally chosen status quo that is hard to unwind. And because this is a multimember expert body with a single layer of protection and no congressional role in removal—precisely the setting where our precedents have been most tolerant—I would not use interim relief to decide, as a practical matter, what should be resolved on a fuller merits record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is equitable: a stay may effectively give the President the benefit of removal before appellate review can test whether “cause” truly existed, potentially frustrating Congress’s independence design. But as the Chief Justice notes, the district court’s order is not mere preservation—it is an affirmative command compelling the President to retain (and not replace) an officer exercising substantial executive authority, a separation-of-powers injury not readily cured by later reversal. On the statutory question, I remain persuaded (as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Alito emphasize) that we should not engraft extra procedural prerequisites or an artificially cramped, “in-office only” gloss onto § 241’s bare “for cause” text; integrity-related material misrepresentations plausibly qualify at least for likelihood-of-success purposes. Granting a stay on that narrow statutory basis avoids any premature Article II resolution while preventing a judicial order from disabling even arguable removal authority during appeal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right to stress the equitable risk that a stay could yield the practical benefits of removal before appellate review, potentially diluting Congress’s independence design. But the injunction here is not merely status-quo preserving; as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, it affirmatively compels the President to retain an officer and disables the President’s core supervisory tool, which is an irreparable Article II injury not later cured by a merits ruling. On likelihood of success, I agree with Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito that we should not infer notice-and-hearing or an unduly narrow, “on-the-job only” gloss from statutory silence, and that alleged material misrepresentations bearing on integrity plausibly constitute “cause” at least enough to justify interim relief. We can grant a stay on that narrow statutory basis without resolving the broader constitutional question about § 241’s tenure protection.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest point from the Chief Justice, Justice Thomas, and Justice Alito is that an injunction barring removal can itself inflict an immediate Article II injury by disabling a key supervisory tool, and I do not discount that concern. But that framing presupposes the President has a plausible statutory entitlement to remove now, whereas the threshold question is the ordinary meaning of § 241’s “for cause” limit; on this record, I am not persuaded the government has shown a sufficiently clear likelihood that the alleged misrepresentations meet that independence-protecting standard rather than functioning as a discretionary pretext, as Justice Kagan emphasizes. A stay would largely confer the practical benefit of removal and replacement before appellate review can determine whether cause existed, risking that interim relief moots meaningful review of Congress’s for-cause design. Given that the constitutional question remains at least debatable under Humphrey’s Executor/Wiener for a multimember body, I would not use interlocutory relief to resolve—practically if not formally—what should be decided on a fuller merits record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s point that an injunction restraining removal can itself impose an Article II harm, but that framing still presupposes that the President is likely acting within the bounds of the removal authority Congress actually conferred in § 241. At this stay posture, the applicants have not made a sufficiently clear showing that the asserted integrity-related misstatements satisfy the historically independence-protecting “for cause” limit—as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize—such that we should effectively award the practical benefit of removal and replacement before appellate review can test legality. Justice Gorsuch’s “narrow statutory” route does not solve that problem; it still turns on a likelihood-of-success determination about what “cause” means in this statutory scheme, and the structure counsels caution rather than deference to an asserted discretionary removal judgment. Equitably, preserving Congress’s designed status quo pending appeal better protects meaningful judicial review than a stay that would be difficult to unwind if the removal is ultimately found unlawful.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article II’s removal power is the rule, and statutory limits are permissible only within narrow, historically bounded exceptions; the Federal Reserve Board’s for-cause tenure, as applied to a Governor who participates in core, ongoing economic policy, strains those exceptions because it insulates an officer exercising substantial executive authority from presidential accountability in a setting unlike the classic Humphrey’s Executor model. In the stay posture, the applicants have at least a substantial likelihood of showing that the President either (i) acted within the statutory “for cause” standard given the alleged material misrepresentations bearing on integrity and fitness for office, or (ii) that the for-cause restriction is unconstitutional as an extension of prior exceptions into a new situation. A preliminary injunction that forces the President to retain a principal officer whom he has found unfit inflicts an irreparable separation-of-powers injury without requiring proof that policy outcomes would have differed absent the restriction. If the for-cause provision is ultimately held invalid, it is severable because the Board’s remaining statutory powers can function independently and nothing in the text or history makes it evident Congress would have preferred no Board at all to one whose members are removable at will.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article II vests “the executive power” in the President, which generally includes the authority to supervise and remove those who exercise executive power in his stead. Federal Reserve Governors exercise substantial executive power—promulgating binding regulations and imposing sanctions—so a statutory for-cause limit that prevents the President from ensuring faithful execution conflicts with Article II, and the Constitution therefore displaces that restriction rather than leaving the President’s removal authority dormant. In the stay posture, a district court order that affirmatively blocks the President’s removal attempt risks leaving the Executive unable to exercise constitutionally required supervisory control and may force continued service by an officer whom the President has determined should be removed, making interim relief appropriate. Because an unconstitutional tenure protection does not automatically “taint” agency action, the narrower and immediate harm here is the injunction’s direct interference with presidential removal, warranting a stay pending appeal.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: At the stay stage, the applicants have made a strong showing that they are likely to succeed at least on the statutory question whether the President had “cause” to remove Governor Cook, and the district court’s injunction improperly deprives the President of the ability to supervise an officer who participates in substantial executive functions, including regulatory and enforcement-related powers. Under Seila Law’s separation-of-powers analysis, for-cause insulation is constitutionally suspect when it constrains the President’s control over officers exercising significant executive power; the Federal Reserve’s multimember structure does not, by itself, place it within Wiener’s narrow adjudicatory exception. Cook’s arguments for additional procedural prerequisites (notice-and-hearing) cannot be inferred from statutory silence; absent clear text, we should not read extra removal constraints into § 241’s “for cause” language. And in equitable terms, maintaining the injunction risks ongoing Article II harm by continuing to block (or at least chill) a removal the President has attempted, whereas any later merits correction can be addressed on remand, consistent with Collins’s insistence that remedies track concrete causation and harm.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Congress here was not silent: 12 U.S.C. § 241 expressly limits removal of Federal Reserve Governors to "for cause," and under longstanding precedent (Humphrey’s Executor; Wiener) that legislative choice to provide independence to a multimember financial regulator is generally permissible and should not be displaced by extending newer, narrower removal cases beyond their facts. Functionally, the Board’s core work—setting monetary policy and supervising aspects of the banking system through an expert, multimember body with staggered terms—does not present the same separation-of-powers concern as a single Director wielding broad unilateral coercive power, and Congress had strong institutional reasons to insulate that work from immediate political control. In the stay posture, allowing removal now would effectively award the President the practical benefit of victory by enabling an immediate replacement and shifting policy influence before appellate review, undermining Congress’s for-cause design and the courts’ ability to provide meaningful relief if the removal is ultimately found unlawful. At most, the President’s allegations go to whether the asserted mortgage-related misrepresentations satisfy the statutory "for cause" standard, not to a wholesale constitutional invalidation of § 241, and that statutory merits dispute does not justify staying the injunction at this stage.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying our longstanding precedent, the Federal Reserve Board’s structure fits comfortably within the Humphrey’s Executor/Wiener category: a multimember, expert body insulated by a single layer of for-cause tenure protection, with no congressional role in removals and no Free Enterprise Fund-style layering problem. In this stay posture, the President has not made a sufficiently clear showing that the asserted “misrepresentations” satisfy the statutory “for cause” standard in the way this Court has traditionally understood that term (as akin to inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office), particularly given the need for notice-and-hearing procedures historically associated with cause removal. And because a stay would effectively deliver the practical benefits of removal before appellate review, the equitable balance—consistent with a causation-sensitive remedial approach—favors leaving the preliminary injunction in place until the courts determine whether the removal restriction and the asserted cause actually mattered to this specific personnel action.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Start with the statute: Congress allowed removal “for cause,” not “only for on-the-job misconduct after appointment” or only after particular procedures the text does not supply. On this record, the President has at least a plausible basis to argue that material misrepresentations bearing on honesty and fitness for office satisfy “cause,” and in the stay posture the government need show a fair prospect of success and irreparable harm from being forced to retain (and be unable to replace) a principal policymaker. Granting a stay can be justified on narrow statutory grounds without deciding the broader Article II question, respecting separation-of-powers limits by avoiding unnecessary constitutional adjudication. Because the injunction effectively prevents the President from exercising even arguable statutory authority over an executive-branch officer during the litigation, the equities favor maintaining the status quo ante pending appeal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 241 contains an express for-cause restriction, so the immediate question in this stay posture is whether the President has shown a sufficient likelihood that the asserted mortgage-related material misrepresentations constitute “cause” (at least serious misconduct or malfeasance) such that the removal is lawful under the statute. Given the Executive’s strong Article II interest in being able to supervise and control high-level officers who exercise significant governmental power, and given the practical irreparability of being forced to retain an officer the President has determined engaged in serious misconduct, a stay is warranted pending appeal. Even assuming Humphrey’s Executor remains controlling as to some multimember expert commissions, that does not eliminate the need to give “for cause” real content while allowing the President to vindicate it when substantial misconduct is credibly alleged; and the equities on a preliminary injunction should not effectively decide the case by freezing the President’s supervisory tools. The injunction should therefore be stayed while the courts determine whether the alleged conduct satisfies the statutory for-cause standard (without needing at this stage to resolve the broader constitutional question about the Fed’s removal protections).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a threshold matter, I would start with the statute’s ordinary meaning: §241’s “for cause” limitation is a real constraint, and on this preliminary record the President has not shown a sufficiently clear, legally reviewable basis that Governor Cook’s alleged mortgage-related misrepresentations constitute “cause” in the sense Congress used to protect Board independence rather than mere policy disagreement or reputational concern. That statutory conclusion matters to the stay posture because the applicants have not carried their burden to show a strong likelihood of success on the merits, and a stay would effectively give the President the practical benefit of removal before appellate review can test whether the asserted “cause” is legally sufficient. Only after that statutory inquiry would I reach the constitutional question, and here the intrusion on Article II supervision is less obviously “conclusive and preclusive” given Congress’s long-settled design of the Federal Reserve as a multimember expert body with for-cause protection; at minimum, that makes this a poor vehicle to override Congress’s scheme via interim relief. Because the equities and public-interest factors cut against mooting meaningful review through immediate replacement, I would deny the stay and leave the preliminary injunction in place pending appeal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The operative text Congress chose—removal only “for cause,” restored in 1935 in the immediate wake of Humphrey’s Executor—signals an enforceable constraint, not open-ended presidential discretion; and the statutory context confirms Congress’s deliberate design to insulate Federal Reserve Governors from policy-driven displacement. In this stay posture, the applicants have not made a sufficiently strong showing that the asserted “cause” (alleged misrepresentations connected to a mortgage) clearly fits the historically understood “for cause”/inefficiency-neglect-malfeasance standard in a way that justifies overriding Congress’s independence-protecting scheme before appellate review. Granting a stay would also effectively moot meaningful judicial review by enabling immediate replacement and attendant policy influence—an interim consequence that is difficult to unwind and that cuts against equitable restraint where Congress has structured an independent, multi-member body. Given the narrowing path available (resolving the dispute on the statutory meaning and application of “for cause” rather than issuing a broad Article II ruling), I would deny a stay and allow the ordinary review process to proceed.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the President may remove a sitting Federal Reserve Board Governor and obtain a stay of a preliminary injunction blocking that removal, notwithstanding statutory "for-cause" removal protections and separation-of-powers limits.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Banking Act of 1935 § 203(b) (Federal Reserve Board governors removable by the President only "for cause"); U.S. Constitution Article II (executive power and Take Care duty) as implicated by removal authority and separation of powers.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The President argues he lawfully removed Governor Lisa D. Cook based on alleged serious misconduct (material misrepresentations related to mortgage rates) that at minimum is grossly negligent and at worst fraudulent, creating an intolerable appearance of impropriety in financial matters; he contends the case can be resolved on the narrower ground that the removal satisfied any applicable "for cause" standard rather than litigating the broader constitutionality of the Fed’s tenure protections, and therefore a stay of the district court’s preliminary injunction is warranted.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Cook (and supporting amici) argue the President’s removal violates Congress’s statutory for-cause limits designed to preserve Federal Reserve independence, and that the district court correctly enjoined the removal; they further contend that granting a stay would effectively decide the dispute in the President’s favor in practical terms (allowing replacement and policy shift before merits review), undermining the statutory scheme and rule-of-law interests, and that longstanding Supreme Court precedent supports meaningful for-cause removal protections for independent agencies.
key_precedents: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make their strongest point in warning that a stay could hand the President a practical endgame before merits review, especially given Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener’s tolerance for for-cause limits in certain multimember expert bodies. But the order we are asked to stay is not merely preservative; as Justice Barrett and Justice Alito emphasize, it affirmatively compels the President to continue retaining an officer he has purportedly removed, inflicting a present, structural Article II injury that cannot be fully unwound later. We can resolve this posture narrowly, as Justice Kavanaugh suggests, by concluding the injunction is likely overbroad given that the alleged material misrepresentations plausibly qualify as “cause” under any ordinary understanding, without deciding whether Humphrey’s Executor ultimately governs this arrangement. On that limited footing, the likelihood of success and balance of harms favor staying the injunction while leaving disputed facts and broader constitutional questions for merits review.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Humphrey’s Executor and the Federal Reserve’s multimember design counsel preserving Congress’s for-cause regime and the “status quo” pending merits review. But the “status quo” here is a judicial injunction that affirmatively blocks a presidential removal and thereby disables Article II supervision now, which—consistent with Justice Alito’s framing—constitutes an immediate separation-of-powers injury independent of downstream questions about severability or any purported “taint.” Even assuming §203(b) applies, Justice Kavanaugh persuasively explains that the alleged material misrepresentations plausibly satisfy any ordinary understanding of “for cause,” making the reinstatement order an overreach at this interim stage. And if the removal restriction is unconstitutional as applied, the defect is the restriction itself; the Constitution controls notwithstanding the statute, so equity should not entrench the very barrier that likely violates Article II.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that a stay may effectively hand the President the practical endgame before merits review by enabling a replacement and policy shift—deserves weight in equity. But, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the district court’s order is not a neutral preservation of the status quo; it is an affirmative command that the President retain an officer he has purported to remove, inflicting a present Article II supervision injury that cannot be fully repaired later. Moreover, Justice Kavanaugh’s narrower statutory point reinforces likelihood of success: on this record, alleged material misrepresentations plausibly fall within any workable understanding of “for cause,” making categorical reinstatement overbroad even without deciding the outer constitutional question under Humphrey’s Executor. Consistent with Seila Law and Collins, the existence of a removal-protection issue and the ultimate remedy are analytically separable, so staying the injunction now appropriately halts ongoing structural harm while leaving factual causation and merits disputes for full review.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett are right that an injunction restraining removal can implicate Article II interests, but that cannot be treated as categorically irreparable when Congress has expressly imposed a historically tolerated for-cause limit on a multimember expert body under Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener. The petitioners’ “narrow statutory” framing—pressed by Justice Kavanaugh—asks us on a stay posture to resolve a contested, fact-bound question whether the alleged misrepresentations meet §203(b)’s for-cause standard, effectively awarding the President the endgame (displacement and replacement) before any court definitively finds “cause.” Under Morrison’s degree-of-interference approach, the single-layer for-cause protection here does not “completely strip” presidential control, and granting a stay would invert ordinary equitable principles by treating immediate, merits-dispositive relief as mere interim management. In short, preserving the status quo pending full review better respects Congress’s structural choice and avoids turning generalized Article II rhetoric into an automatic stay rule, as Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson caution.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett make the best point for petitioners: an injunction compelling retention can itself burden Article II supervision. But that harm cannot be treated as categorically irreparable where Congress has long used (and this Court has long tolerated) a single-layer, presidential-only for-cause protection for multimember expert bodies, and where the asserted “cause” is genuinely disputed on this record. Justice Kavanaugh’s proposed “narrow” route would, at the stay stage, effectively decide a merits-laden statutory/factual question—whether the alleged misrepresentations are categorically sufficient—and thereby hand the President the practical endgame (replacement) that is hard to unwind if removal later proves unlawful. Under Morrison’s degree-of-interference inquiry, this arrangement does not “completely strip” removal authority, so the equitable balance still favors maintaining the injunction pending full review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that a stay effectively hands the President the practical endgame before merits review—has force, but it cannot obscure that the district court’s order is not a passive preservation of the status quo; it is an affirmative judicial command compelling the President to retain an officer he has purportedly removed, inflicting a here-and-now Article II injury to supervision and accountability. That sort of structural harm is not the counterfactual, after-the-fact inquiry I have criticized elsewhere (whether a President “would have” removed), but a present disablement of removal authority, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress. And as Justice Kavanaugh notes, the alleged material misrepresentations plausibly satisfy any ordinary understanding of “for cause,” making the reinstatement injunction appear overbroad even on statutory grounds without resolving the constitutional question. On a stay posture, we should not treat judicially enforced insulation as the equilibrium when it itself trenches on the separation of powers in real time.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the strongest point that a stay can hand the President the practical endgame by enabling a replacement and near-term policy shift that may be hard to unwind. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the district court’s order is not merely preserving a prelitigation status quo; it is an affirmative injunction compelling the President to retain an officer he has purportedly removed, imposing a present Article II supervision injury while merits disputes play out. On the narrower statutory path, I agree §203(b) clearly adopts a for-cause standard, yet the alleged material misrepresentations plausibly fit ordinary meanings of “malfeasance” or “neglect of duty,” and the statute does not clearly demand trial-like procedures before removal—making categorical reinstatement likely overbroad at this stage. Under Nken, that likelihood-of-success showing, plus the ongoing structural injury from compelled retention, justifies a stay without resolving whether Humphrey’s Executor should be extended in this setting.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan are right that a stay may allow replacement and policy change that is difficult to unwind, so we should not treat interim relief as a merits shortcut. But the district court’s order is not merely preservative; it affirmatively compels the President to retain a principal officer he has purported to remove, producing an ongoing separation-of-powers injury to Article II supervision that is not fully cured by later merits review (as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito stress). At this posture we can grant a stay on the narrower ground Justice Kavanaugh identifies: the asserted “material misrepresentations” plausibly qualify as “cause” under the ordinary meaning of §203(b), making the reinstatement injunction likely overbroad without deciding whether Humphrey’s Executor ultimately governs the Federal Reserve’s modern structure. Under Nken, that likelihood-of-success showing combined with the irreparable institutional harm from judicially compelled retention supports a stay pending appeal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s contention that an injunction compelling retention imposes an immediate institutional cost on Article II supervision. But that asserted harm is largely derivative of Congress’s concededly applicable for-cause regime for this multimember expert body—one our precedents have long tolerated—and it does not justify converting generalized separation-of-powers concerns into a near-automatic stay rule that displaces ordinary equitable balancing. Justice Kavanaugh’s proposed “narrow” statutory path still asks us, at the stay stage, to credit contested allegations as sufficient “cause” under §203(b) and thereby deliver the practical endgame (removal and replacement) before any court finally resolves that merits-laden, fact-bound question. Given the asymmetry in remedies (replacement now is difficult to unwind if the removal is unlawful), I would leave the district court’s interim relief in place pending orderly review rather than disable effective judicial redress.

John Roberts.reasoning: The President’s removal authority is the constitutional rule, and statutory limits are valid only within narrow, already-recognized exceptions; extending Humphrey’s Executor to insulate Federal Reserve Governors—officers who wield substantial policymaking and enforcement-adjacent authority affecting the Nation’s economy—would push that exception into a new context our recent cases have approached with skepticism. At this stage, the President has at least a strong likelihood of showing either that the asserted misconduct satisfies any applicable “for cause” standard or that the for-cause restriction is unconstitutional as applied, making a stay appropriate to prevent ongoing intrusion on Article II supervision while merits review proceeds. If the for-cause protection is ultimately invalid, the proper remedy is to sever that restriction while leaving the remainder of the Federal Reserve framework intact, as it can function independently and nothing suggests Congress would have preferred no Board at all to one whose members are removable at will. Any remaining disputes about the precise factual basis for “cause,” or the effect of subsequent ratification by accountable officials, can be addressed on remand after full merits proceedings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: A Federal Reserve Board Governor exercises significant executive power through regulatory, supervisory, and enforcement authority, and Article II therefore requires that the President be able to supervise and remove such an officer. Section 203(b)’s “for cause” restriction is, at minimum, constitutionally suspect as applied here, and any statutory limit that conflicts with the President’s Article II removal authority must yield to the Constitution rather than redefining the Governor as outside the Executive Branch. On the stay request, the district court’s preliminary injunction affirmatively blocks the President’s removal, creating a serious separation-of-powers harm and raising the distinct concern that continued service may rest on an unlawful judicial constraint on presidential control; that favors a stay pending merits review. Even assuming a for-cause standard applies, the President has at least a substantial argument that alleged material misrepresentations in sensitive financial matters constitute “cause,” further supporting likelihood of success and the equitable case for a stay.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A stay is warranted because the President has made a strong showing that this removal can be sustained on the narrow statutory ground that it was "for cause": if the alleged material misrepresentations in a financial-matters context are proven, they readily qualify as at least gross negligence or malfeasance, and a "for cause" standard cannot be treated as a trivial constraint when it would otherwise bar removal for disobedience of lawful presidential direction. Even if the Court ultimately concludes that §203(b)’s tenure protection is unconstitutional as applied to a Federal Reserve Governor who participates in nonadjudicatory, policymaking and supervisory functions, that constitutional defect is analytically separable from remedy; the preliminary injunction itself inflicts concrete harm by preventing the President from exercising Article II supervision now. Consistent with Collins and Seila Law, the proper course is to allow removal pending merits review and leave factual and causation disputes (including whether the asserted misconduct occurred and whether the restriction altered executive control or the challenged actions) for further proceedings rather than locking in a judicially enforced barrier to removal at the outset.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Congress did not remain silent here: it expressly limited removal of Federal Reserve Board Governors to "for cause" in §203(b), a structural choice long recognized as constitutionally permissible for multimember expert bodies insulated to carry out nonpartisan, stability-oriented functions. Under Humphrey’s Executor and Wiener, that kind of tenure protection for a multimember commission is part of the settled constitutional landscape, and Seila Law’s "significant executive power" concerns are weaker where the official is one member of a bipartisan, multimember board designed to be independent rather than a single Director wielding unilateral coercive authority. On the stay request, the equities and status quo favor maintaining the district court’s injunction: a stay would effectively decide the case by permitting immediate replacement and policy reorientation before merits review, while the President’s asserted harm is speculative given available supervisory tools short of removal and the unresolved factual dispute whether the alleged misstatements satisfy a true for-cause standard. Granting a stay on this record would also continue the Court’s recent doctrinal drift that discounts Congress’ authority to structure the Executive Branch and treats presidential removal interests as categorically overriding even when Congress has clearly spoken.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 203(b) gives the President only a for-cause removal power over a Federal Reserve Governor, and under Humphrey’s Executor and Morrison the question is functional: whether that limit so interferes with Article II as to "impede the President’s ability to perform his constitutional duty." A single, presidential-only for-cause restriction—especially in a long-standing financial-regulator design like the Fed’s—does not "completely strip" the President of control; it preserves accountability while protecting institutional independence that Congress has historically deemed essential. On this stay posture, the President has not made a sufficiently clear showing that the alleged misrepresentations establish for-cause removal as a matter of law or that immediate displacement is necessary to avert irreparable Article II harm, while granting a stay would effectively award the practical relief (replacement and policy shift) before merits review. Given that the statute’s structure involves no congressional role and no multilayer insulation (so Free Enterprise Fund concerns are not triggered), the balance favors enforcing the for-cause regime pending full adjudication.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: A statutory scheme that purports to forbid the President from removing an officer who exercises significant executive power inflicts a separation-of-powers injury immediately, because it disables presidential supervision that Article II makes the linchpin of democratic accountability. On the facts alleged here—serious misconduct involving material misrepresentations in a role central to financial governance—the President has at least a strong likelihood of showing “cause” even assuming § 203(b)’s for-cause limit applies, and the district court’s injunction improperly prevents the Executive from effectuating removal while merits review proceeds. A stay does not require courts to indulge counterfactual speculation about whether the President “would have” removed the Governor absent the restriction; the constitutional harm from insulation is a here-and-now impairment of lawful supervision, and the traditional remedy is to permit the President to act rather than freeze the Executive Branch in place. Given Article II’s structural command and this Court’s recent removal precedents, the equities and likelihood of success favor staying the injunction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 203(b) contains an express for-cause standard, so this case can and should be resolved on that narrower statutory ground rather than by expanding or contracting Humphrey’s Executor. On the stay posture, the President has shown a substantial likelihood of success that the alleged material misrepresentations in a financial-matters context qualify at least as “malfeasance” or “neglect of duty” (or, at minimum, serious misconduct) within any reasonable understanding of “for cause,” and the Executive’s Article II interests in supervision of high-level officers weigh heavily in the balance of equities. Because the preliminary injunction effectively disables the President’s removal authority pending litigation, it imposes a significant separation-of-powers harm that cannot be fully remedied after the fact, supporting a stay while merits review proceeds. Given that Congress spoke clearly to require cause—but not to require the most demanding, trial-like adjudication before removal—the President’s showing here is sufficient to justify removal and a stay of the injunction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: In this interim-relief posture, the question is whether to stay the preliminary injunction, not to definitively resolve the constitutionality of § 203(b)’s for-cause protection for Federal Reserve Governors. Applying Nken, the President has shown a substantial likelihood of success on the narrower ground that the asserted misconduct—material misrepresentations bearing directly on financial integrity—fits comfortably within any ordinary-meaning conception of “for cause,” making the district court’s categorical reinstatement order likely overbroad. The injunction also inflicts irreparable separation-of-powers harm by compelling the President to retain (and continue supervising) a principal officer he has determined should be removed, intruding on core Article II supervisory authority while effectively freezing executive staffing decisions pending merits review. Given those harms and the limited role of equitable relief, a stay is warranted without deciding whether Humphrey’s Executor should extend to the Federal Reserve in the modern administrative state.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Congress expressly authorized Federal Reserve Board Governors to be removed only “for cause,” and the district court’s task at the preliminary-injunction stage is to preserve the statutory scheme while the merits are adjudicated, not to let the Executive effectively nullify it through interim relief. On this record, the President’s asserted “misconduct” rationale is, at minimum, contested and merits-bound, and granting a stay would functionally hand the Executive the ultimate relief (displacement and replacement) before any court can determine whether the statutory for-cause standard was actually met. The separation-of-powers framing does not justify that result in this posture because applying § 203(b) as written is not Congress criminalizing or disabling an executive prerogative so much as Congress structuring an independent multimember body in a manner long accepted by this Court. Consistent with the Judiciary’s rule-of-law role and equitable authority to provide effective relief against unlawful removals, I would deny the stay and leave the injunction in place pending merits review.
